# Installing Gkeyll and postgkyl {.unnumbered}

You will install two things:

- **Gkeyll**, the simulation code. We build only its `core` and `moments`
  layers, which contain the multi-fluid solvers used in these lectures.
- **postgkyl**, the Python package for reading and plotting Gkeyll output,
  together with [marimo](https://marimo.io) for the lecture notebooks.

The instructions below have been tested on macOS (Apple silicon) and on
Ubuntu 24.04. On Windows, first install the
[Windows Subsystem for Linux](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install)
with `wsl --install`, then follow the Linux instructions inside the Ubuntu
terminal it provides.

Expect the whole installation to take 10 to 30 minutes, depending on your
laptop (most of it is spent building Gkeyll's dependencies), and to use about
3 GB of disk space.

## 1. Prerequisites

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

Install Apple's command-line developer tools (compilers, `git`, `make`):

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

Install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) if you do not already have it, then use it
to install CMake:

```bash
brew install cmake
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential gfortran cmake clang git curl rsync
```

:::

Finally, install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which we use to set up
Python (it works the same way on both systems):

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Open a new terminal window afterwards so that the `uv` command is found.

## 2. Build Gkeyll

Download the source code into your home folder:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll.git
cd gkeyll
```

### Dependencies

Gkeyll needs a few libraries (SuperLU, OpenMPI, LuaJIT, and on Linux,
OpenBLAS). The `install-deps` script downloads and builds them into
`~/gkylsoft`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
export MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=$(sw_vers -productVersion | cut -d. -f1-2)
cd install-deps
./mkdeps.sh --build-superlu=yes --build-openmpi=yes --build-luajit=yes --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft
cd ..
```

The first line tells the LuaJIT build which version of macOS to target (your
own); without it, LuaJIT does not build.

## Linux / WSL

```bash
cd install-deps
./mkdeps.sh --build-openblas=yes --build-superlu=yes --build-openmpi=yes --build-luajit=yes --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft
cd ..
```

:::

The script keeps going even if one library fails to build, so check that
they are all there before moving on:

```bash
ls ~/gkylsoft
```

You should see `luajit`, `openmpi`, and `superlu` (plus `OpenBLAS` on Linux),
along with a few versioned folders. If one is missing, scroll back through the
script's output to find the error.

### Configure and compile

Configure the build for the moments solvers only (`--app=moments`), with MPI
for running in parallel and Lua for reading input files:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
./configure --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft --use-mpi=yes --use-lua=yes --app=moments
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
./configure CC=clang --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft --use-mpi=yes --use-lua=yes --mpi-inc=$HOME/gkylsoft/openmpi/include --app=moments
```

:::

Then compile and install. The number after `-j` is how many files to compile
at once; use the number of cores in your laptop, or fewer if it has less than
16 GB of memory:

```bash
make install -j 4
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Linux on an ARM processor

If your Linux machine has an ARM processor rather than an Intel or AMD one
(for example a Windows laptop with a Snapdragon chip, or a Linux virtual
machine on an Apple silicon Mac; check with `uname -m`, which prints
`aarch64`), the moments solver currently fails to compile with errors about
`xmmintrin.h`. Run this from the `gkeyll` folder, then `make install -j 4`
again:

```bash
sed -i 's/defined(__arm64__) || defined(__powerpc64__)/defined(__arm64__) || defined(__aarch64__) || defined(__powerpc64__)/' core/zero/gkyl_dflt.h
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How this differs from Gkeyll's own instructions

Gkeyll's README builds with "machine files" such as
`./machines/mkdeps.macos.sh`. Those build every solver (including the much
larger kinetic and gyrokinetic ones) and download atomic data that only the
gyrokinetic solver uses. The commands above build the same dependencies but
only the solvers these lectures need.
:::

### Add Gkeyll to your path

Tell your shell where the `gkeyll` and `mpirun` commands live. On macOS, add
this line to `~/.zshrc`; on Linux and WSL, add it to `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin:$HOME/gkylsoft/openmpi/bin:$PATH"
```

Open a new terminal and check that it worked:

```bash
gkeyll -v
```

You should see something like:

```
This is the Gkeyll code. See gkeyll.rtfd.io for details.
Type 'gkyl -h' for help.

Built with git changeset "d1aa4ef33ec7"
Built on "2026-10-11 22:01:46 UTC"
Built without CUDA
```

## 3. Install postgkyl and marimo

Download these lectures, which include the notebooks and simulation input
files, and create a Python environment inside the lecture folder:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/JunoRavin/reconnection-lectures.git
cd reconnection-lectures
uv venv --python 3.12 --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Download postgkyl next to the lectures and install it, together with marimo,
into that environment. Installing postgkyl compiles a small extension that
connects it to Gkeyll's data format, so this step takes a minute or so:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/gkeyllorg/postgkyl.git ../postgkyl
uv pip install ../postgkyl marimo
```

Whenever you come back to the lectures in a new terminal, reactivate the
environment from inside the `reconnection-lectures` folder with
`source .venv/bin/activate`.

## 4. Check your installation

Gkeyll comes with a small version of the GEM reconnection problem that the
lectures study. Run it in a scratch folder (this takes well under a minute):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/gkeyll-check && cd ~/gkeyll-check
cp ~/gkeyll/moments/luareg/rt_10m_gem.lua .
gkeyll rt_10m_gem.lua
```

When it finishes, the folder contains `.gkyl` output files. With the lecture
environment active, load the final electromagnetic field with postgkyl:

```bash
python -c "import postgkyl as pg; print(pg.load('rt_10m_gem-field_1.gkyl').get_values().shape)"
```

This should print

```
(128, 64, 8)
```

that is, the field on the 128 × 64 grid of this test problem, with eight
components: the three components each of the electric and magnetic fields, and
two potentials Gkeyll uses to keep the divergence constraints satisfied.

If you see this, everything is installed and you are ready to
[run the simulations](running.qmd).
